ap_statistics-m02.stem: A random sample of $500$ voters is used to find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of all voters who support a proposal. The sample proportion is $0.52$, and the conditions for inference are met. The interval is $(0.476,\ 0.564)$. Does the interval provide convincing evidence for the claim that a majority of all voters support the proposal?

options.text: Yes, because the sample proportion $0.52$ is greater than $0.5$.
options.why: Judges the claim from the sample proportion alone; the interval shows how far the population proportion can be from the sample proportion.

options.text: No, because the interval $(0.476,\ 0.564)$ includes values on both sides of $0.5$, so $0.5$ is a plausible value.
options.why: An interval that includes the value leaves it plausible, so the claim that the proportion is greater than that value is not supported.

options.text: Yes, because most of the values in the interval $(0.476,\ 0.564)$ are greater than $0.5$.
options.why: The claim is justified only if all of the plausible values satisfy it; most of them is not enough.

options.text: Yes, because a $95\%$ interval always provides convincing evidence for a claim about a proportion.
options.why: An interval supports a claim only when the value in the claim is not a plausible value; the confidence level alone does not decide this.

ap_statistics-m02.stem: A random sample of $200$ customers is used to find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of all customers who prefer the new recipe. The sample proportion is $0.48$, and the conditions for inference are met. The interval is $(0.411,\ 0.549)$. Does the interval provide convincing evidence for the claim that more than $40\%$ of all customers prefer the new recipe?

options.text: No, because the sample proportion $0.48$ is not equal to $0.4$.
options.why: The sample proportion never has to equal the value in the claim; the interval shows which population proportions are plausible.

options.text: Yes, because every value in the interval $(0.411,\ 0.549)$ is greater than $0.4$, so $0.4$ is not a plausible value.
options.why: A claim that the proportion is greater than a value is supported when the whole interval lies above that value, so the value itself is not plausible.

options.text: No, because a confidence level of $95\%$ is too low to support any claim about a proportion.
options.why: A $95\%$ interval is commonly used to support claims; the claim is judged by comparing the interval with the value.

options.text: No, because the interval $(0.411,\ 0.549)$ is not centered at $0.4$.
options.why: An interval is not required to be centered at the value in the claim; what matters is whether the value is inside the interval.

ap_statistics-m03.stem: A least-squares regression line for predicting the number of cups of hot chocolate sold from the temperature, in degrees Celsius is $\hat y = 94.5 - 3.84x$, based on data for which $x$ ranges from $0$ to $15$, with $r = -0.91$. A researcher uses the line to predict number of cups when $x = 34$. Which of the following statements about the prediction is correct?

options.text: The prediction of $-36.1$ is reliable, because the correlation of $0.91$ is close to $1$.
options.why: A strong correlation within the range of the data does not make predictions outside that range reliable.

options.text: The prediction of $-36.1$ is an extrapolation, because $34$ is outside the range of the data, so the linear pattern may not continue and the prediction may be unreliable.
options.why: Predictions for values of the explanatory variable outside the range of the data assume that the linear pattern continues, which the data cannot confirm.

options.text: The prediction of $-36.1$ is reliable, because the line is the least-squares line, which has the smallest sum of squared residuals.
options.why: The least-squares property describes the fit to the observed data, not the behavior of the relationship outside the data.

options.text: The prediction cannot be made, because a regression line can only be used for the values of $x$ that appear in the data set.
options.why: A prediction can be calculated for any value of $x$; the issue is that it is unreliable outside the range of the data.
